stem: A US insurer's security review of a claims assistant adds two requirements: model inference must run only on US infrastructure, and uploaded files and other data stored at rest by the Claude API must also stay in the US. No individual developer should be able to send a request that runs elsewhere. The team currently uses an existing workspace with default settings. Which plan meets the requirements?

options.text: Add inference_geo set to "us" to every request in the client code and document the rule in the team's coding standards.
options.why: This controls where inference runs but not where data is stored at rest, and it relies on every developer remembering the parameter.

options.text: Create a new workspace with workspace geo "us", and restrict its allowed inference geos to "us" only.
options.why: Workspace geo governs data at rest and is fixed at workspace creation; allowed_inference_geos makes the API reject any request that asks for another geo.

options.text: Change the workspace geo of the existing workspace to "us" in the Console, then keep sending requests as before.
options.why: Workspace geo is chosen when a workspace is created and cannot be changed afterward, and it does not control where inference runs.

options.text: Enable zero data retention for the organization so that no request data is stored outside the United States.
options.why: Retention policy controls how long data is kept, not the geography of inference or storage; residency needs the geo controls.

explanation: Data residency on the Claude API has two independent controls. Inference geo (the inference_geo parameter, a workspace default, or an allowed_inference_geos restriction) decides where model inference runs; workspace geo, set only when a workspace is created, decides where data is stored at rest and where endpoint processing happens. A requirement covering both, enforced rather than left to developers, maps to a new US workspace whose allowed inference geos are limited to "us".
reference: Claude API docs — Data residency (inference geo, workspace-level restrictions, workspace geo)

stem: A team calls the Messages API from Go with a hand-written HTTP client. It decodes responses with strict decoding that rejects unknown JSON fields, and its switch statements over stream event types and stop_reason return an error for any value they do not recognize. One morning parsing starts failing in production, although the anthropic-version header and the code have not changed. What is the best fix?

options.text: Pin an older anthropic-version header so the API stops returning fields and values that the client does not expect.
options.why: Within a version, Anthropic may add output fields and new enum variants, so an older header does not freeze the response shape; older versions are also deprecated.

options.text: Treat the unexpected responses as an API bug and retry each failed request with backoff until it parses cleanly.
options.why: The responses are valid under the versioning policy, so retrying returns the same shape and keeps failing.

options.text: Make the client a tolerant reader: ignore unknown fields and add a default branch for unknown enum values.
options.why: The versioning policy allows added output values and new enum-like variants such as event types, so clients should handle unknown ones gracefully.

options.text: Always send the newest anthropic-version header so the client automatically understands any fields that are added.
options.why: The header selects API behavior; it does not teach a strict client to parse fields or values that its own code rejects.

explanation: For a given anthropic-version, Anthropic preserves existing inputs and outputs but may add optional inputs, add output values, and add new variants to enum-like outputs such as streaming event types. Robust JSON clients are tolerant readers: they ignore unknown fields and route unknown enum values to a default branch instead of failing. The official SDKs already do this.
reference: Claude API docs — Versions; Streaming messages (event types)

stem: A platform team rolls Claude Code out to 300 engineers through Amazon Bedrock. Engineers launch sessions with the opus and sonnet aliases. Some engineers see fallback notices because the alias pointed to a model not yet enabled in their AWS account, and the team wants model upgrades to happen only when it decides. What should the team do?

options.text: Keep using the aliases, since on Bedrock they always resolve to the newest Anthropic model as soon as it is released.
options.why: On third-party providers the aliases resolve to a built-in default that can lag new releases and may not be enabled, and it can change on a Claude Code update.

options.text: Set the ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_*_MODEL variables to version-specific Bedrock model IDs and change them to upgrade.
options.why: The documented practice is to pin version-specific provider model IDs before rollout, so the team controls when users move to a new model.

options.text: Set the variables to Claude API model IDs such as claude-opus-4-8, since the same ID strings work on every provider.
options.why: Model ID formats differ by provider; Bedrock uses its own IDs, such as us.anthropic.claude-opus-4-8.

options.text: Add a line to the project CLAUDE.md telling Claude which Opus and Sonnet versions every session should use.
options.why: CLAUDE.md is instruction context; it cannot choose the model a session runs on.

explanation: When Claude Code is deployed through Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, Microsoft Foundry, or Claude Platform on AWS, pin model versions before rollout by setting ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL, ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL (and the Haiku and Fable equivalents) to version-specific IDs in the provider's format. Upgrading then becomes a deliberate change to those variables followed by a redeploy.
reference: Claude Code docs — Model configuration (Pin models for third-party deployments)
